name: Linear A
signs: c. 90 syllabic signs plus logograms and numerals

claims.text: Linear A was used on Crete from c. 1800 to 1450 BC.
Linear B was adapted from Linear A.
The language recorded is not Greek.
Approximate phonetic values can be assigned from Linear B correspondences.
The underlying language can be identified with a known language family.

summary: The script of Minoan Crete — readable in sound but not in meaning, because the language behind it is unknown.
body:
Linear A is a syllabary of about 90 signs plus logograms for commodities and a decimal number system including fractions. It appears on clay tablets, sealings, and — unusually — on stone libation vessels and gold and silver objects, so it was used for religious dedication as well as accounting.

We can pronounce much of it. Linear B was adapted from Linear A, so shared signs presumably kept similar values, and applying them to Linear A texts produces sound-sequences. But those sequences are not Greek, not Semitic, and not convincingly anything else. Around 1,400 documents survive, most of them very short, which is far too small a corpus for statistical decipherment.

Proposals connecting the language to Luwian, Etruscan, Phoenician and others have all failed to convince. Without a bilingual text or a much larger corpus, it is likely to stay unread.

name: Linear B

claims.text: Linear B records an early form of Greek.
It was deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952.
All known Linear B texts are administrative records.
The script represents Greek phonology imperfectly.
Literacy in Linear B was confined to palace administrators.
Michael Ventris was a professionally trained architect and self-taught amateur, not an academic linguist, when he deciphered the script.
The American classicist Alice Kober's pre-war grid analysis of recurring sign patterns supplied essential groundwork that Ventris built directly on.

summary: The earliest form of written Greek — a syllabary badly suited to the language, used only for palace accounting.
body:
Linear B writes Greek with a syllabary evidently designed first for some other, unrelated language, and the fit is genuinely poor. The script cannot distinguish *l* from *r*, has no consistent way to mark aspiration, and regularly drops final consonants, so a sign group transliterated *pa-te* could in principle represent either *patēr* (father) or *pantes* (all) — reading any given tablet requires constant contextual judgement rather than straightforward transcription, which is part of why the decipherment took as long as it did once scholars finally had enough tablets to work with.

Every one of the thousands of surviving tablets is a piece of palace administration, and nothing else. They record flocks and the shepherds responsible for them, wool quotas owed to the palace, allocations of bronze for smiths, chariot wheels specifically noted as serviceable or broken, rations issued to groups of women textile workers together with their children, and offerings to named gods including, on tablets from both Knossos and Pylos, an early form of Zeus. There is no literature, no history, no law code and no private correspondence anywhere in the corpus — the tablets are disposable annual accounts, most surviving only because the palace buildings that stored them burned, baking the unfired clay hard enough to last three thousand years by accident.

The decipherment itself, achieved in 1952, is one of the genuine intellectual triumphs of twentieth-century scholarship, and it was accomplished largely outside professional academia. Michael Ventris was a trained architect by profession, not a career linguist, who had been fascinated by the mystery of the undeciphered Aegean scripts since meeting Arthur Evans as a schoolboy in 1936, and who worked on the problem essentially as a private obsession alongside his day job. He built directly on painstaking earlier groundwork by the American classicist Alice Kober, who had died in 1950 without cracking the script herself but whose systematic grid analysis, tracking which signs regularly changed together in ways consistent with grammatical case endings, gave Ventris the structural scaffolding he needed. Working from a similar grid organising signs by probable shared consonants and vowels without assuming what any individual sign actually sounded like, Ventris noticed that testing a cluster of signs as probable Cretan place names produced coherent results only if the underlying language was Greek — a conclusion he found so unexpected, given the prevailing assumption that Linear B recorded some lost non-Greek Minoan language, that he initially argued against his own emerging result before the evidence became impossible to resist.

When the Mycenaean palaces that used it collapsed at the end of the Bronze Age, the script vanished with them almost without trace, and Greece would not be reliably literate again for several centuries, using an entirely different, alphabetic script borrowed from the Phoenicians. Linear B was never a language of literature, religion or law in its own right; it was a tool built for and by palace bureaucracy, and it had no life at all outside the palace walls that generated it.

name: The Greek alphabet
signs: 24 letters in the standard Ionic form

claims.text: The Greek alphabet was adapted from a Phoenician consonantal script.
Unused Phoenician consonant signs were reassigned as vowels.
Greek letter names are meaningless in Greek but meaningful in Semitic languages.
The Latin alphabet descends from a western Greek variant via Etruscan.
Athens adopted the Ionic alphabet officially in 403 BC.

summary: The first writing system to represent both consonants and vowels — adapted from Phoenician by repurposing unneeded signs.
body:
Phoenician script recorded consonants only. That works for Semitic languages, where roots are consonantal and vowels are predictable, but it fails for Greek, where vowels carry essential distinctions.

The Greek solution was to take Phoenician letters for sounds Greek did not have — the glottal stop *aleph*, the pharyngeal *ayin*, *he*, *yod* — and reassign them as alpha, omicron, epsilon and iota. The letter names came along untranslated: *aleph* means "ox" and *beth* means "house" in Phoenician, and mean nothing at all in Greek. That is itself proof of the borrowing.

The result could represent any Greek word unambiguously and could be learned in weeks rather than years. Local alphabets varied at first — Athens used a different set from Corinth or Euboea — until Athens adopted the Ionic standard in 403 BC.

The Euboean variant travelled to Italy and became Etruscan, then Latin, and so the alphabet used for most of the world's writing today.

name: Koine Greek
status: Ancestor of Byzantine and Modern Greek

claims.text: Koine Greek developed primarily from Attic with Ionic influence.
It became the administrative and commercial lingua franca of the Hellenistic world.
Greek inscriptions of Ashoka survive at Kandahar in Afghanistan.
The Septuagint and New Testament are written in Koine.
Greek remained dominant in the eastern Mediterranean under Roman rule.

summary: The simplified common Greek that spread with Alexander's conquests and became the lingua franca from Marseille to the Indus.
body:
Koine — "common" — grew out of Attic Greek with Ionic influence, spreading through Alexander's armies and administration. It simplified: the dual number disappeared, the optative mood declined, the dative began eroding, and vocabulary standardised.

It was the first genuine lingua franca of the Mediterranean and Near East. A merchant from Massalia and an official in Babylon could do business in it. Inscriptions in Koine turn up in Afghanistan and India — the Ashoka edicts at Kandahar are in Greek and Aramaic, so a Buddhist emperor addressed his Greek-speaking subjects in their own language.

It is also the language of the Septuagint and the New Testament, which is why the vocabulary of a Hellenistic Greek administrative culture became the vocabulary of Christian theology.

Rome conquered the Greek world without displacing it linguistically. Greek remained the language of the eastern Mediterranean for a further thousand years.

name: The Achaemenid Empire

claims.text: The Achaemenid Empire extended from the Aegean to the Indus at its greatest extent.
Darius I organised it into satrapies with fixed tribute obligations.
The Royal Road connected Sardis to Susa with relay stations.
Administrative tablets record rationed wages paid to male and female workers.
Greek accounts of Persia are systematically shaped by hostility.
The Cyrus Cylinder records Cyrus the Great permitting displaced peoples, including Judean exiles in Babylon, to return home and restore their own temples.
The elite infantry corps the Greeks called the "Immortals" was kept permanently at a strength of 10,000 by immediately replacing any casualty.

summary: The largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from the Aegean to the Indus, and the defining external power in Greek history.
body:
Founded by Cyrus the Great around 550 BC, the Achaemenid Empire eventually governed perhaps 25 million people — a substantial fraction of humanity alive at the time — across the Balkans, Egypt, Anatolia, Mesopotamia, Iran and Central Asia, making it by a wide margin the largest state the world had yet seen. Cyrus set the tone for how it would rule from the start: the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay proclamation issued after his conquest of Babylon, records him permitting displaced peoples, including Judean exiles held in Babylon, to return to their homelands and rebuild their own temples — a policy of restoring rather than erasing conquered peoples' institutions that some modern commentators have controversially compared to an early human-rights charter, and that in any case gave the empire's early conquests real practical legitimacy in the eyes of those it absorbed.

Its administrative achievement was genuine and durable. Darius I divided the empire into satrapies, each with a fixed tribute obligation and a Persian governor typically balanced by independent royal inspectors the Greeks called "the King's Eyes and Ears," standardised a gold coin called the daric, and built the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, its relay stations allowing couriers on the royal messenger system to cover roughly 2,700 kilometres in about a week — a speed of long-distance communication nothing else in the ancient Mediterranean world matched. Local languages, religions, legal codes and even local rulers were generally left in place under this system rather than replaced with Persian equivalents; the empire governed through administered diversity rather than enforced uniformity, an approach that let it hold together dozens of previously independent kingdoms and cultures for two centuries. Its military reflected the same scale: the elite infantry corps the Greeks called the "Immortals," after the Persian custom of instantly replacing any casualty so the unit's paper strength of 10,000 never visibly changed, became one of the most recognisable images of Persian power in Greek accounts of the wars between the two.

Those Greek accounts are, however, almost the entirety of what popular memory of Persia is actually built on, and they are systematically hostile, written by people with an obvious interest in explaining and dignifying a Greek military victory against overwhelming numerical odds. Persian administrative sources tell a considerably less lurid story: the Persepolis Fortification tablets, an enormous cache of everyday bureaucratic records rather than royal propaganda, show ordinary wages paid in grain, wine and other rations to workers of both sexes on the palace's own payroll, including specific extra rations recorded for women who had recently given birth — the routine texture of an administered state rather than the despotic caricature that dominates Herodotus and later Greek tradition.

Alexander the Great destroyed the empire's political independence in a single sustained campaign between 334 and 330 BC, defeating Darius III in three major battles and burning the ceremonial capital of Persepolis, but he then governed much of the conquered territory using the Achaemenid empire's own administrative machinery largely intact, retaining Persian satraps and Persian methods of taxation and communication rather than replacing them wholesale — an implicit acknowledgment that the system Cyrus and Darius had built worked well enough to be worth keeping, even for the man who had just destroyed the dynasty that built it.

name: The Ptolemaic Kingdom

claims.text: The Ptolemaic dynasty ruled Egypt from 305 to 30 BC.
The Ptolemies presented themselves as pharaohs to Egyptians and Greek kings to Greeks.
Key commodities including grain, oil and papyrus were royal monopolies.
The dynasty practised sibling marriage.

summary: Greek-ruled Egypt under Alexander's general Ptolemy and his descendants — the wealthiest and longest-lasting successor kingdom.
body:
The Ptolemies governed Egypt for 275 years as a Greek-speaking elite over an Egyptian population, presenting themselves as pharaohs to Egyptians and as Hellenistic kings to Greeks. Temple reliefs show them in pharaonic dress making offerings to Egyptian gods; their coins show them in Greek royal diadems.

The economy was tightly controlled. Grain, oil and papyrus were state monopolies, and Egypt's agricultural surplus made the kingdom enormously rich — wealth that funded the Library, the Museum and the Pharos.

The dynasty practised sibling marriage, following Egyptian royal precedent, which produced a genealogy of extraordinary complexity and a great deal of murder within the family.

Cleopatra VII was the last. Her defeat at Actium and death in 30 BC ended the kingdom and the Hellenistic age with it.

name: The Seleucid Empire

claims.text: The Seleucid Empire was the largest of Alexander's successor states.
The Seleucid Era, beginning 312/311 BC, was the first continuous numbered year-count.
The Seleucids founded numerous Greek cities across Asia as instruments of control.
The empire lost its eastern provinces progressively to Parthia and Bactria.

summary: The largest successor state, inheriting most of Alexander's Asian conquests from Anatolia to Central Asia.
body:
Seleucus I took Babylonia in 312 BC — the year from which the Seleucid Era counts, making it the first continuous numbered year-count in history and the ancestor of all such systems, including AD dating.

The empire's problem was its size and diversity. It governed Greeks, Babylonians, Persians, Jews, Bactrians and dozens of other peoples, and held them together by founding Greek cities as anchors of control — Antioch, Seleucia-on-the-Tigris, Apamea, Laodicea and many more.

It lost territory steadily: the far east to the Mauryans and then to the Parthians, Bactria to a breakaway Greek kingdom, and Anatolia to Rome after Magnesia in 190 BC. The attempt to impose Greek practice in Judaea under Antiochus IV provoked the Maccabean revolt.

Pompey annexed what remained in 63 BC.

name: Crete

claims.text: Crete was settled by farming populations arriving by sea around 7000 BC.
It hosted Europe's first palace-based state society.
Its position linked Aegean, Egyptian and Levantine trade routes.

summary: The largest Greek island, home of Europe's first palace civilisation and a crossroads between the Aegean, Egypt and the Levant.
body:
Crete is 260 km long, mountainous, and positioned where the sea routes from Egypt, the Levant and the Aegean converge. That position explains most of its history.

It was settled by around 7000 BC by farmers who brought livestock and crops by boat — one of the earliest maritime colonisations known. The palaces emerged around 1900 BC and dominated the Aegean until the destructions of 1450 BC.

After the Bronze Age it became comparatively marginal: a land of many small poleis, known for archers, mercenaries and, in the standard Greek stereotype, lying. The "Cretan paradox" — a Cretan saying all Cretans are liars — enters logic and eventually the New Testament.

Rome took the island in 69–67 BC.

name: The Cyclades

claims.text: Melian obsidian was traded across the Aegean from the Mesolithic onwards.
Parian and Naxian marble supplied Greek sculpture throughout antiquity.
Early Cycladic culture produced distinctive marble figurines c. 3200–2000 BC.

summary: The ring of Aegean islands around Delos — source of marble, obsidian and the earliest distinctive art of the Aegean.
body:
The name means "the circle", from the islands ringing sacred Delos. They are small, dry, and individually poor, which made their inhabitants exceptional sailors: everything had to move by sea.

Their resources mattered. Melos supplied obsidian across the Aegean from the Mesolithic. Paros and Naxos supplied the white marble used for Cycladic figurines and later for the finest Greek sculpture — the Nike of Samothrace and the Venus de Milo are both Parian.

The Early Cycladic culture of 3200–2000 BC produced the folded-arm figurines and the engraved "frying pans", and maintained trade networks that later Minoan and Mycenaean powers inherited.

Thera, at the southern edge, erupted catastrophically around 1600 BC.

name: Cyprus

claims.text: Cypriot copper was mined and exported across the Mediterranean from the Bronze Age.
The Latin cuprum ("copper") derives from the island's name.
Cyprus was divided among roughly ten city-kingdoms with mixed Greek and Phoenician populations through the Archaic and Classical periods.
Cyprus returned to stable Ptolemaic control by the 290s BC and remained so until 58 BC.
Cyprus was restored to Ptolemaic rule from 48 to 30 BC after its first Roman annexation.

summary: A copper-rich island facing the Levant, divided among small Greek–Phoenician city-kingdoms and later secured as one of the Ptolemies' most valuable possessions.
body:
Cyprus sits close enough to the Levantine coast to trade with it constantly and far enough offshore to develop on its own terms. Its copper mines supplied the Bronze Age Mediterranean; the Latin word for the metal, *cuprum*, derives from the island's name rather than the other way round.

Through the Archaic and Classical periods it was never one state but around ten small city-kingdoms — Salamis, Paphos, Kition, Kourion and others — with mixed Greek and Phoenician populations, nominally subject to Assyria, then Egypt, then Persia, while their own kings struck coins and fought each other. That fragmentation made the island a prize rather than a power in its own right.

After Alexander's death it was fought over repeatedly. Demetrius Poliorcetes broke Ptolemaic control of it at Salamis in 306 BC, but Ptolemy I recovered the island by the 290s BC, and his dynasty held it as a core possession — naval base, copper and timber supply — for over two centuries. Rome annexed Cyprus in 58 BC; Ptolemaic rule was restored from 48 to 30 BC before the island returned permanently to Roman control.

name: The Hittite Empire

claims.text: Hittite archives refer to a power called Ahhiyawa across the sea.
They name a city Wilusa in north-west Anatolia and a king Alaksandu.
Hattusa was destroyed and abandoned around 1190 BC.
Ahhiyawa refers to Mycenaean Greeks.
Wilusa is Homeric Ilios and Alaksandu is connected to Alexandros/Paris.

summary: The Anatolian great power whose archives name Mycenaean Greeks — and whose collapse is the clearest marker of the Bronze Age crisis.
body:
The Hittites ruled central Anatolia from Hattusa and fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh around 1274 BC, producing the earliest surviving peace treaty, of which both Egyptian and Hittite copies exist.

For Greek history their archives are decisive. They record a land called Ahhiyawa across the sea, whose king is treated at times as a great king and equal — generally identified with a Mycenaean Greek power. They also name Wilusa, plausibly Homeric *(W)ilios*, and a king of Wilusa called Alaksandu, which sits uncomfortably close to Alexandros, the alternative name of Paris.

This is the only external written evidence for the Mycenaean world, and it comes from an empire that Greek tradition entirely forgot.

Hattusa was burned and abandoned around 1190 BC.
